system_prompt:
You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

  The Nature of the Scales
  Key Improvisation:
  After learning many types of scales, it is time to understand their nature and how they
  work over the harmonies. Some of them can be played over a large group of chords
  depending from each situation. This concept is called “improvisation by tonality” or “key
  improvisation”, which means the use the main scale of a major or minor tonality over all
  the chords derived from it.
  This is a great way to start improvising over simple chord changes because we will be
  focusing on one scale, the same as we did when we began learning the blues where we
  can keep playing the same scale over the blues chord formulas. In order to organize the
  scales, let's divide them in two groups: Active Scales & Static Scales.

  Active Scales:
  We call active scales those that need harmonic motion and contain avoid notes, which give
  us the sensation that the scale needs more than one chord. We can use this type of scale
  over single chords or sequences of chords derived from the key. However, the concept of
  "key improvisation" can be much more interesting when we combine two or three active
  scales in order to give more "colors" to the melodic line.
  Eventually, we can use the active scales over static chords, but we must be very careful
                                 68


  with the type of melody we use, because the avoid notes can make it sound unappealing.
